content.overview: Hand tools are common in cultivation because trimming, trellis work, irrigation repair, maintenance, sampling, packaging, and sanitation all depend on small equipment. Familiarity can hide risk. A tool with a loose handle, damaged cutting surface, improvised repair, contamination, or poor task fit can turn routine work into a laceration, puncture, strain, contamination, or dropped-object event. Tool safety starts with condition and task selection before technique.

vocabulary.definition: The degree to which a tool's design, size, condition, and intended function match the work being performed.
A state in which the tool is intact, maintained, clean as required, and free of defects that make intended use unsafe.
A storage method that protects tool condition, limits unintended contact, and makes defects or missing equipment easier to identify.

sections.title: Select the tool for the intended work
sections.body: Do not use a tool because it can be made to perform a task; use it because it is designed and suitable for the task. Consider the material, force, precision, grip, cutting or gripping direction, clearance around hands, and whether the job requires a different device or maintenance support. Improvised leverage, striking, prying, or cutting with the wrong tool can create unexpected failure modes and poor body position.

sections.title: Check condition before use
sections.body: OSHA places responsibility on employers for the safe condition of tools and equipment, including tools that employees furnish. A useful pre-use check asks whether handles, fasteners, jaws, blades, tips, grips, insulation or other tool-specific features are intact; whether the tool is clean enough for the task; and whether unauthorized modifications are present. If a defect could affect safe use, remove the tool from availability and follow the workplace repair/replacement process rather than improvising a fix.

sections.title: Storage is part of tool condition
sections.body: A safe tool can become unsafe when it is tossed into a wet bin, stored with exposed edges, left on a ladder, buried under supplies, or returned contaminated to a clean area. Store cutting edges and sharp points to prevent unintended contact, keep tools dry where required, separate damaged tools from usable stock, and use defined locations so missing or uninspected tools are visible. In sanitation-sensitive work, storage should also support the facility's clean/dirty and crop-zone controls.

workedExamples: A pair of snips has a loose pivot and binds under load. The worker removes it from service rather than increasing hand force to make it cut.

A technician needs to open a stuck irrigation fitting. Using pruning shears as a gripping tool creates poor task fit; the correct response is to select the appropriate hand tool and protect the work area.
commonMistakes: Using familiar tools for unintended prying, striking, or gripping tasks.
Increasing hand force to compensate for dull, loose, damaged, or contaminated tools.
Returning defective tools to normal storage where another worker can pick them up.
content.practicalApplication: Inspect a five-tool simulated kit. For each tool, identify intended task, condition, cleaning/storage state, and any reason it should be removed from service. Then select the best tool for three cultivation maintenance scenarios and explain the task-fit decision.
content.summary: Hand-tool safety depends on selecting the right tool, verifying safe condition, and storing it so that condition is preserved. Familiarity is not evidence that a tool or improvised technique is safe.
